sections.title: Nodes 0–1 — The problem, and the first annotation
sections.content:
Where this sits

This is the base of the chain. Node 0 is the world without TypeScript and the four specific ways it fails; Node 1 is the smallest possible response — writing down what a value is and having a program check it. Every later node is a consequence of decisions made here, and two of them — that checking happens before the program runs, and that the checker only ever reads your code — are assumptions the rest of the topic never revisits.

Every term, from absolute zero

Program — a text file of instructions that a machine can carry out. You write it; something else executes it. The gap between those two moments is where this entire topic lives.

Runtime — the period when your program is actually executing, and by extension the software doing the executing. When someone says "at runtime," they mean "while the program is running, with real values flowing through it." A runtime error is one that only appears then.

Compile time — the period before your program runs, when some tool is processing your source text. A compile-time error is found by reading, without executing anything. The entire value proposition of TypeScript is moving errors from the first category to the second.

Value — an actual piece of data your program holds: the number 42, the text "devansh", a list, an object. Values exist at runtime. They are the things that are real.

Type — a description of a set of values, together with what you're allowed to do with them. number is the type describing all numeric values, and it permits arithmetic. string describes all text values, and it permits things like uppercasing. A type is not a value; it's a claim about which values can appear somewhere. This distinction sounds pedantic and is the single most important idea in the topic — types describe, values exist.

Type system — the rules that decide which types are compatible with which, and therefore which programs are allowed. Two languages can both have a type called string and still disagree about what may be assigned to it.

Static typing — checking types by reading the source code, before running it. "Static" here means "not moving" — nothing is executing while the check happens.

Dynamic typing — checking types while the program runs, at the moment an operation is attempted. JavaScript is dynamically typed: it happily lets you write "hello" * 3, and only when that line executes does it produce NaN, meaning "not a number."

JavaScript — the language browsers run, created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995. It is dynamically typed, which is the situation Node 0 describes.

JavaScript engine — the program that actually executes JavaScript. V8 is the one inside Google Chrome and inside Node.js. It has no knowledge of TypeScript whatsoever, and this fact constrains everything.

Node.js — a way to run JavaScript outside a browser, released in 2009, built on V8. It's what makes JavaScript usable for servers, and it's why backend jobs ask about this language at all.

Annotation — a note attached to something. A type annotation is a note in your source code saying what type a value is: let count: number = 0. The colon-and-type is not JavaScript; it's TypeScript's addition.

Inference — working something out rather than being told it. Type inference is when the compiler determines a type from context: you wrote let count = 0, so the compiler concludes count is a number without you saying so.

Compiler — a program that reads source code and produces something else, usually source code in another language or a form the machine can run. tsc — TypeScript Compiler — is TypeScript's, and it does two separable jobs: checking your types and emitting JavaScript.

Transpile — compile from one language to another language at a similar level of abstraction, rather than down to machine instructions. TypeScript to JavaScript is transpiling. The word is a contraction of "transform" and "compile," and you can treat it as a synonym for what tsc does when it writes output.

Emit — the compiler's output step. "TypeScript emits JavaScript" means it writes .js files. A flag called noEmit tells it to check without writing anything, which is a mode you will use constantly.

Source file extension — .ts is a TypeScript file, .js is JavaScript. .tsx and .jsx are the variants that permit JSX, the HTML-looking syntax React uses. The extension is what tells the tooling which rules apply.

Syntax — the arrangement of characters a language accepts as well-formed. let x = ; is a syntax error: it's not that the meaning is wrong, it's that it isn't a sentence.

Token — the smallest meaningful piece of source text: a keyword like let, a name like count, a symbol like =. Splitting text into tokens is the first thing any compiler does, and it's called lexing or tokenising.

AST — Abstract Syntax Tree — the tree-shaped structure a compiler builds from tokens, representing the program's grammatical structure. "Abstract" because it drops incidental detail like whitespace; "syntax tree" because a program nests — a function contains statements, a statement contains expressions, an expression contains other expressions. Every tool that understands code rather than merely searching it works on an AST.

Symbol — a compiler's internal record of a named thing: this count here is the same count as that one over there. Building that map is called binding, and it's what makes "rename every use of this variable" possible without text search.

Language server — a background program that provides code intelligence to an editor: what type is this, where is it defined, what can I type next. TypeScript's is called tsserver, and it is the same codebase as tsc running in a different mode. When your editor shows a type on hover, tsserver computed it. This matters more than it sounds: the editor experience is not a separate feature bolted onto TypeScript — it is the compiler, answering questions interactively.

LSP — Language Server Protocol — a standard, published by Microsoft in 2016, for how editors talk to language servers. It's why TypeScript works identically in VS Code, Neovim and JetBrains editors rather than needing a plugin written three times.

Autocomplete — the editor offering valid continuations as you type. With types, the list is correct rather than guessed, because the compiler knows exactly what properties a value has.

Refactoring — changing the structure of code without changing what it does: renaming, extracting a function, changing a signature. Safe refactoring requires knowing which occurrences of a name refer to the same thing, which requires symbols, which requires types.

Gradual typing — a type system designed so that a codebase can be partly typed and partly not, with the two coexisting. This was a hard design requirement for TypeScript, not a nicety, and it explains the existence of any (Node 9) and the file-by-file adoption story below.

Literal type — a type inhabited by exactly one value. The type "devansh" contains only the string "devansh". It sounds useless in isolation and becomes essential at Node 4.

Widening — the compiler generalising a literal type to its base type: "devansh" becoming string. It happens when a value could later be reassigned, and understanding when it happens is most of understanding inference.

The history — why this exists at all

JavaScript was written in ten days in May 1995 to make web pages interactive, and for its first decade nobody expected it to be used for anything large. A typical script was a few dozen lines: validate a form, swap an image on hover. At that size, dynamic typing is not a problem. You can hold the whole program in your head, and a mistake surfaces the moment you reload the page.

Three things changed that, in order.

Gmail, in 2004. Google shipped an email client that ran inside a browser and behaved like a desktop application, using a technique that came to be called AJAX — the browser fetching data in the background without reloading the page. It demonstrated that serious applications could live in a browser, and it was tens of thousands of lines of JavaScript. Google Maps followed the next year. The demonstration was successful enough to be a problem: JavaScript was now being used at a scale it had never been designed for.

jQuery and the library era, from 2006. A shared ecosystem grew, meaning that most of the code in an application was now written by strangers, and the only description of how to call it was documentation written by hand.

Node.js, in 2009. JavaScript escaped the browser and became a server language, which meant that codebases now had backends in the same untyped language, maintained for years by rotating teams.

By around 2010 the pain was concrete and widely felt, and several serious attempts were made to fix it. It's worth knowing what they were, because TypeScript's design is a direct reaction to why they failed.

Google Closure Compiler (open-sourced 2009) took the approach of writing types in comments — a convention called JSDoc, where you annotate a function with @param {string} name above it — and then reading those comments to check and optimise the code. This has a real virtue: the file remains valid JavaScript, so nothing needs compiling to run. It has a fatal one too, which is that comments are second-class. The syntax is verbose, expressing anything complicated is painful, and no editor of the era gave you a decent experience with it. Notably, this idea did not die — JSDoc-based typing is still supported by TypeScript today, and it's what checkJs uses.

GWT (Google Web Toolkit, 2006) took the opposite approach: write Java, compile it to JavaScript. Script# did the same for C#. These give you a real type system, and they fail because you're no longer writing JavaScript — you can't easily use JavaScript libraries, you can't read the output, and every browser API needs a hand-written wrapper before you can touch it.

CoffeeScript (2009) compiled a nicer syntax to JavaScript and was briefly very popular, but added no types at all.

Dart (Google, 2011) was the most aggressive attempt: a new language intended to replace JavaScript in browsers outright, with Google planning to ship a Dart virtual machine in Chrome. Other browser vendors declined, the plan was abandoned in 2015, and Dart survives today as the language of Flutter. Its failure is the clearest evidence for the constraint that shaped TypeScript: you cannot replace JavaScript, because you cannot replace every browser in the world.

Microsoft had the problem acutely and internally. Bing Maps and the Office web applications were enormous JavaScript codebases maintained by large teams, and the company had spent years watching its own developers struggle. In 2010 an internal project codenamed Strada was started under Anders Hejlsberg — a designer with an unusual pedigree, having created Turbo Pascal in the 1980s, been chief architect of Delphi, and then designed C# at Microsoft from 2000. His prior work is all in the nominal, statically-typed tradition, which makes the choices he made here more interesting rather than less.

The project's founding constraints were, in effect, the lessons from every failure above. It must be a superset of JavaScript — every valid JavaScript file must be a valid TypeScript file, so adoption costs nothing on day one and you can rename a file and start. It must compile to readable JavaScript that runs everywhere, with no runtime library. It must interoperate with untyped libraries, since the ecosystem is the reason to be on this platform at all. It must be adoptable file by file, because no team can stop shipping to convert a codebase. And — this is the one people underrate — it must make the editor good, because the daily experience of autocomplete and go-to-definition is what actually gets a tool adopted by developers who are not persuaded by arguments about correctness.

TypeScript 0.8 was announced on 1 October 2012, open source under the Apache 2.0 licence. The reception was initially mixed; the argument that "JavaScript doesn't need types" was widely made at the time and looks very strange now. Version 1.0 arrived in April 2014.

Two events decided it. In March 2015, the Angular team at Google announced that Angular 2 would be written in TypeScript — a competitor adopting Microsoft's language, which is an unusual endorsement and instantly gave TypeScript an enormous professional audience. And DefinitelyTyped, a community repository of hand-written type declarations for untyped JavaScript libraries, grew large enough that the ecosystem problem largely solved itself; you'll meet it properly at Node 12.

The main rival was Flow, released by Facebook in 2014 with a more theoretically rigorous type system. TypeScript won, and the reasons are instructive: better editor integration, a far larger declaration ecosystem, sustained investment, and a willingness to be pragmatically unsound in exchange for describing real-world JavaScript — a trade you'll meet repeatedly from Node 6 onward. Flow still exists and is used inside Meta; outside it, TypeScript is effectively the default.

Version 2.0, in September 2016, added strictNullChecks, which is Node 5 and is arguably the single most valuable feature the language ever shipped. Everything after that is refinement, and the language is still adding — satisfies in 4.9 (2022), erasableSyntaxOnly in 5.8 (2025), and a rewrite of the compiler in Go announced in 2025 that you'll meet at Node 19.

The mechanism — traced

Here is what actually happens when you run tsc on a file. Four phases, in order.

Phase one: scanning. The file is read as text and split into tokens. let count: number = 0; becomes the token sequence let, count, :, number, =, 0, ;. Whitespace and comments are dropped, apart from a few special comments the compiler cares about — // @ts-ignore, for one.

Phase two: parsing. The tokens are assembled into an AST according to the grammar. That statement becomes a variable statement node, containing a declaration list, containing one declaration whose name is count, whose type node is the keyword number, and whose initialiser is the numeric literal 0. Everything downstream operates on this tree, not on your text. This is why TypeScript can rename a variable reliably where text search cannot: it's working on structure, and it knows that count in a string literal is not the same thing as the variable.

Phase three: binding. The compiler walks the tree and builds symbols and scopes — the map of what names exist where, and which references point to which declaration. Scope is nesting: a name declared inside a function is visible inside it and not outside. Binding is what makes "find all references" mean something.

Phase four: checking. This is where types happen, and it's worth being precise about how, because it demystifies the whole thing. The checker walks the tree and computes a type for every expression, then verifies that each operation is permitted for the types involved.

For let count: number = 0, it does three things: reads the annotation and records that count's declared type is number; computes the type of the initialiser 0, which is the numeric literal type 0; and checks assignability — is 0 assignable to number? Yes, because the literal type 0 is a subset of number. If you had written "five", the check fails and you get the error.

Now the same statement without the annotation: let count = 0. There's no declared type, so the compiler must infer one. It computes the initialiser's type — again the literal type 0 — and then applies widening, because count was declared with let and could be reassigned later. The literal type 0 widens to number. Had you written const count = 0, no reassignment is possible, so no widening happens and the type stays exactly 0.

That widening rule is worth stating on its own, because a surprising amount of later behaviour is downstream of it: let widens literals to their base type; const keeps them literal. It's why const mode = "dark" has type "dark" and can be used in a discriminated union at Node 4, while let mode = "dark" has type string and cannot.

Inference then flows outward through expressions. const doubled = count 2 — the checker knows count is number, knows the numeric literal 2 is a number, knows on two numbers yields a number, so doubled is number. Nothing magical is happening; each rule is small and they compose.

For calls into libraries, the same process consults declarations that ship with TypeScript. "a,b".split(",") works because TypeScript includes a declaration file describing every method on String.prototype, including that split returns string[]. These files are called lib files — lib.es2015.d.ts and friends — and which ones are included is a configuration decision you'll meet at Node 13.

Phase five: emitting. The compiler writes JavaScript. For our statement, let count: number = 0; becomes let count = 0;. The annotation is deleted and nothing takes its place. That deletion is erasure and it is Node 2's whole subject; for now, notice only that the emitted line is the line you'd have written by hand.

And now the behaviour that catches everyone once: by default, phase five happens even if phase four found errors. tsc reports the errors and writes the JavaScript anyway. This looks like a bug and is a deliberate decision from the adoption constraints — a team migrating a large codebase has thousands of errors on day one and still needs to ship. The flag noEmitOnError turns it off. In practice most modern projects sidestep the question entirely by never using tsc to build at all, which is Node 14.

One more mechanism belongs here, because it's half of TypeScript's actual value: the editor runs the same compiler. When you hover a variable in VS Code, tsserver has already parsed, bound and checked your project, and it answers from the same type information tsc would produce. When you type a dot, it lists the properties of the computed type. When you rename, it uses the symbol table from binding. This is why the editor experience is correct rather than heuristic, and it's why a type error in your editor and a type error in CI are the same error from the same code — assuming both are using the same TypeScript version and the same config, which is a caveat that will eventually bite you and is worth remembering as a diagnostic.

Where should you actually write annotations, given all this inference? The rule is: annotate where information enters the program, and let inference carry it through. Function parameters, because there's nothing to infer from — the compiler cannot know what callers will pass. The shapes of external data. Everything else, leave alone. A file dense with annotations is usually a file where someone has written down what the compiler already knew, and those written-down facts then rot exactly like the stale comments from Node 0.

In your project

Stage 1 of recast is built precisely on this node, and deliberately in the awkward order: you write the first converter in plain JavaScript, get it working, and make a mistake you only find by running it. That's not ceremony — the four failures of Node 0 are things you have to feel once, and feeling them takes ten minutes.

The migration then follows the historical adoption path rather than a rewrite. You'll set allowJs and checkJs, which is TypeScript reading your JavaScript files and inferring types from them without you renaming anything — the direct descendant of the Closure Compiler idea, now built in. The errors it reports at that stage are pure Node 1: inference discovering what it can and telling you where it can't reach.

The spec warns that the hard part of Stage 1 is the binary type zoo — File, Blob, ArrayBuffer, Uint8Array — and that difficulty is worth naming as a Node 1 phenomenon specifically. It isn't your code being hard to type. It's that those types come from lib files describing browser APIs designed across two decades by different committees, and inference can only report what those declarations say. Your first real experience of TypeScript's difficulty will be at the boundary between other people's declarations, which is where it usually lives.

In qbank

qbank is already TypeScript, and this is the first place to be precise about what that does and doesn't mean. Its tsconfig.json was generated or copied rather than reasoned about, so the project has a dialect nobody chose (Node 13). More to the point for this node: everywhere qbank has an annotation on data coming from Postgres, from an HTTP request, or from the Anthropic API, that annotation is doing exactly what this node describes — making a claim the compiler will check internally for consistency — and nothing more. It reads as safety and is only bookkeeping. That gap is Node 15, and the reason to name it here is that the confidence you currently have looking at that code is the specific thing this topic will replace with something warranted.

What an interviewer does with this

"What is TypeScript?" — asked in almost every screen, and treated as a warm-up, which is exactly why a precise answer stands out. Weak: "JavaScript with types." Strong: "It's a superset of JavaScript that adds a static type layer checked before the code runs and erased in the output, so what actually executes is ordinary JavaScript with no runtime cost. It was designed to be adoptable file by file into existing codebases, which is why it's structural rather than nominal and why any exists."

"Does TypeScript make my code slower?" — a trap for people who think it's a runtime thing. The answer is no, because nothing of TypeScript survives compilation; the only costs are build time and, if you set a low target, less efficient downlevelled syntax.

"What's the difference between a type annotation and type inference, and which should you prefer?" — the answer they want is that you annotate at the boundaries and infer everywhere else, with the reasoning: annotations you write are claims that can go stale, while inferred types stay honest as the code changes. Mentioning that exported public API functions are the exception — explicit return types protect the contract and improve compile speed — is a senior-sounding detail that happens to be true.

"If tsc reports type errors, does it still produce JavaScript?" — a question that separates people who have configured a build from people who have only used one. Yes by default, controlled by noEmitOnError, and in most real projects the point is moot because a transpiler builds and tsc --noEmit gates separately in CI.

"Why didn't the industry just use a typed language instead?" — this is really asking whether you understand constraints rather than trivia. The answer is Dart: Google tried exactly that, could not get a virtual machine into browsers it didn't control, and gave up in 2015. You cannot replace JavaScript, so the only viable solution was one that compiles to it.

sections.title: Node 2 — Structural typing and erasure
sections.content:
Where this sits

Node 1 gave you a compiler that reads annotations and checks them. This node answers the two questions that were left hanging: what does the compiler compare against what, when it decides an assignment is legal, and what happens to all of it once the program actually runs. Structural typing and erasure are the two facts every subsequent node quietly assumes. Almost every surprise later in this topic — excess property errors, branded IDs, why generics can't construct anything, why Zod exists at all — is one of these two showing up somewhere you weren't expecting it.

Every term, from absolute zero

Member — anything a type declares: a property or a method. { name: string; greet(): void } has two members.

Property — a named slot on an object holding a value. user.name reads the property name.

Method — a property whose value is a function, usually called with the object as context. The distinction matters more than it looks; at Node 6 you'll learn that TypeScript checks method parameters by different rules than function-valued properties.

Shape — informal but standard: the set of members a type has, with their types. "Same shape" means same members, same types.

Assignability — the compiler's central question: given a value of type A, may it be used where type B is expected? Every type error you will ever see is ultimately an assignability failure. The relationship is directional — Dog may be assignable to Animal without the reverse being true.

Subtype and supertype — A is a subtype of B if every A is acceptable as a B. Dog is a subtype of Animal; Animal is its supertype. TypeScript's actual rule is assignability rather than strict subtyping — the two mostly coincide, and where they diverge is because of the deliberate holes you'll meet from Node 6 onward.

Structural typing — compatibility is decided by shape alone. If a value has the members the target type requires, with compatible types, it fits. Nothing needs to be declared.

Nominal typing — compatibility requires a declared relationship by name: this class implements that interface, this type extends that one. "Nominal" is from the Latin nomen, name. Java, C#, Rust and Swift work this way.

Duck typing — the dynamic-language version of the same instinct: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." The program doesn't ask what something is, it just calls the method and finds out at runtime whether that worked. The phrase entered programming vocabulary through the Python community around 2000. Structural typing is duck typing checked in advance — that one sentence is the cleanest way to hold the distinction.

Freshness — TypeScript's internal term for an object literal written directly at an assignment or call site, as opposed to a value that has been through a variable. Freshness is what triggers excess property checking, and it is the only reason that check appears to contradict structural typing.

Excess property check — the rule that a fresh object literal may not carry properties the target type doesn't declare, even though structurally extra properties are harmless.

Type identity — whether two types are considered the same type. Under structural typing, two separately declared types with identical members are the same type for all practical purposes, which is exactly the property that branded types work around.

Branded type / phantom type — a structurally-typed value made artificially incompatible by intersecting it with a marker member that exists only in the type system. Used to make UserId and PostId stop being interchangeable. "Phantom" because the member is never present at runtime.

Erasure — deleting the type layer during compilation, leaving no trace in the output. Borrowed vocabulary from Java, which erases generic type arguments (see the history below), though TypeScript erases far more.

Type-directed emit — a compiler generating different runtime code depending on type information. TypeScript almost never does this, and the few places it does are the source of a specific family of problems at Nodes 11 and 19.

Downlevel — rewriting newer syntax into older equivalent syntax so it runs on older engines. Separate from erasure: erasure removes types, downlevelling rewrites JavaScript features.

Prototype — JavaScript's inheritance mechanism. Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype, and property lookups that fail on the object continue up that chain. Classes in JavaScript are a syntax on top of this.

instanceof — a JavaScript operator asking whether a constructor's prototype appears in a value's prototype chain. It is a runtime check, it predates TypeScript, and it only knows about things built from constructors or classes.

typeof — a JavaScript operator returning a short string describing a value's basic kind: "string", "number", "boolean", "undefined", "object", "function", "symbol", "bigint". Eight possible answers, and famously typeof null is "object", which is a bug from 1995 that can never be fixed. Note that TypeScript also has a typeof used in type position which is a completely different operator — Node 10.

Reflection — a program inspecting its own structure at runtime: what type is this, what properties does this class have. Java and C# have rich reflection. JavaScript has almost none, and TypeScript adds none.

Serialisation — converting a value into a transmittable form, usually JSON text, and back. The round trip destroys prototypes and class identity, which is why instanceof stops working on anything that crossed a network, a queue, or a worker boundary.

Soundness — a type system is sound if it never accepts a program that will commit a type error at runtime. TypeScript is deliberately not sound, and the reasons are one of the most interesting things you can say about it in an interview.

Top type / bottom type — a type that every value belongs to (unknown, and unsafely any), and a type that no value belongs to (never). Defined properly at Node 9; mentioned here because assignability is what makes them meaningful.

The history — why this exists at all

Two decisions, made for two different reasons, at roughly the same moment.

Why structural

Hejlsberg's background, as Node 1 covered, is thoroughly nominal — Turbo Pascal, Delphi, C#. In C#, if you want a class to be usable where an interface is expected, you write class User : IUser and the compiler enforces it. Nothing else will do; a class with identical members but no declaration is a different, incompatible thing. This is a good design when you control the whole program, because it means compatibility is intentional, and accidental shape collisions can't create accidental substitutability.

Applied to JavaScript, it fails immediately, and it's worth seeing exactly how. Consider the JavaScript that existed in 2012:

function drawPoint(p) {
  ctx.moveTo(p.x, p.y);
}
drawPoint({ x: 10, y: 20 });
drawPoint(someLibrary.getCursorPosition());
drawPoint(new Vector2(3, 4));

Three different origins for the argument: an object literal written inline, a value from a third-party library, and an instance of a class. Under nominal rules, describing this function would require every one of those to have been declared as implementing some Point interface. The object literal can't be — it's created on the spot. The library value can't be — the library was written before your interface existed and doesn't know about it. The class could be, but only if you own the class and are willing to edit it. A nominal TypeScript would have been able to describe almost no existing JavaScript, which would have made it useless for its actual purpose.

Structural typing dissolves the problem: drawPoint(p: { x: number; y: number }) accepts all three, because all three have an x and a y. No declaration, no coordination, no editing anyone else's code. That's what makes it possible to write type declarations for a library you didn't write, years after it was published — which is the entire basis of DefinitelyTyped at Node 12.

Microsoft published a design-goals document for TypeScript that is unusually candid, and two lines from it explain more than any commentary: among the non-goals are "apply a sound or 'provably correct' type system" and "aggressively optimise the runtime performance of programs." The type system was explicitly built to be useful rather than correct, and that trade is the theme of this entire topic.

Why erasure

The second decision has a different motivation, and it's a reaction to specific failures.

GWT and Script# compiled Java and C# to JavaScript, and the output was machine-generated code nobody could read, with a runtime library shipped alongside to emulate the source language's semantics. Debugging meant reading generated JavaScript that didn't resemble what you wrote. Dart planned to ship a whole virtual machine into browsers. Every one of these made the compiled artefact a foreign object in the JavaScript ecosystem.

TypeScript's constraint was the opposite: the output must be JavaScript a JavaScript developer would recognise as their own code. No runtime library, no helper functions unless downlevelling genuinely requires them, no performance overhead, nothing to install. That way, adopting TypeScript is reversible — you can always run the output, read it, debug it, and if the project fails you still have your JavaScript. It also means TypeScript can never be blamed for a performance regression, which removes the most common objection to a new tool.

Full erasure is what that constraint implies. If types produced any runtime artefact — a shape descriptor, a runtime check, a registry — the output would stop being idiomatic JavaScript and would carry a cost.

The word itself comes from Java. When Java added generics in 2004 (Java 5), it erased the type arguments at compile time so that List<String> and List<Integer> both became plain List in the compiled output. Java did this for backward compatibility with pre-generics code, and it's widely considered a wart there, because it produces the famously irritating situation where you cannot ask, at runtime, what a list contains. TypeScript erases for a different reason and far more aggressively — but the consequence is the same, and it's the consequence that matters: the type layer is gone before the program starts.

There is one historical exception worth knowing, because it explains a class of confusion. Early TypeScript included features that do emit runtime code — enums, namespaces, parameter properties — and later added emitDecoratorMetadata, which is the one place TypeScript deliberately writes type information into the output, emitting a design:type record that frameworks like NestJS and TypeORM read at runtime to do dependency injection and column mapping. These are genuine exceptions to erasure, they're the reason the erasableSyntaxOnly flag exists (Node 19), and they're why "TypeScript is fully erased" needs the qualifier "except for a handful of legacy constructs" if you want to be precise.

The mechanism — traced

How assignability is actually decided

When the checker asks "is source type S assignable to target type T?", for object types it does roughly this: for every member of T, look for a member of the same name in S; if it's missing and not optional, fail; if it's present, recursively check whether S's member type is assignable to T's member type. Members present in S but absent from T are ignored.

Read that last clause again, because it's the whole of structural typing in one line: extra members are irrelevant. The target says what is required, not what is permitted.

interface Point { x: number; y: number }

class Vector2 {
  constructor(public x: number, public y: number) {}
  add(other: Vector2) { /* ... */ }
}

const v = new Vector2(3, 4);
const p: Point = v;   // fine

Vector2 has never heard of Point. It has extra members. It's a class and Point is an interface. None of that matters: it has an x that's a number and a y that's a number, so it's assignable. In C# this would be an error; here it's not even a question.

The comparison recurses through nested objects, and the compiler caches results, because a naive structural comparison of two deeply nested types would be expensive — which is a first hint of Node 18, where this cost becomes something you have to measure.

The consequence you'll actually trip over

If shape is everything, then two types with the same shape are the same type:

type UserId = string;
type PostId = string;

function getUser(id: UserId) { /* ... */ }

const postId: PostId = "post_123";
getUser(postId);   // no error, and this is a real bug

There is nothing for the compiler to object to. Both are string. The names exist only for human readers, and the compiler does not read names.

The fix is a branded type, and understanding why it works is a good test of whether structural typing has landed:

type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" };
type PostId = string & { readonly __brand: "PostId" };

& is intersection (Node 3): a value must satisfy both sides. Nothing that is merely a string has a __brand property, so no plain string is assignable to either, and UserId and PostId are now mutually incompatible because their __brand types differ. At runtime the property doesn't exist and nothing enforces it — you create branded values through a function that asserts the brand once, and that function is the single place the lie lives. Structurally impossible types, faked into existence by a member that never exists. This is the pattern the landscape calls out for money amounts and IDs, and it's what Stage 8 of recast uses.

There is also one accidentally nominal feature worth knowing: classes with private or protected members compare by declaration identity, not structurally. Two classes with identical members, both declaring private id: string, are not assignable to each other, because the compiler tracks which declaration that private member came from. It's the one corner of TypeScript that behaves nominally, and it occasionally explains an error message that otherwise looks impossible.

Freshness and the excess property check

Given all the above, this looks like a contradiction:

interface Options { width: number }

const a: Options = { width: 10, height: 20 };
//                              ~~~~~~ error: 'height' does not exist in type 'Options'

const raw = { width: 10, height: 20 };
const b: Options = raw;   // no error

Same object, two different outcomes. The rule: an object literal written directly at the assignment or argument position is fresh, and fresh literals get the extra check. Assigning it to a variable first launders the freshness away, and ordinary structural rules apply.

Why the special case exists is a good story about pragmatism. Structurally, extra properties are harmless — nothing will read them. But in practice a fresh literal with an unrecognised property is almost always one of two mistakes: a typo (heigth), or a property you think is being used and isn't (passing timeout to a function whose option is called timeoutMs). Both are silent failures of exactly the kind Node 0 exists to prevent. So the compiler carves out an exception where the false-positive rate is low, and leaves the general rule alone. It is not a principle; it is a heuristic that pays for itself.

Knowing the freshness rule also tells you how to work around the check honestly when you do want extra properties: assign to a variable first, or widen the target type, rather than reaching for as (Node 9), which switches off checking rather than expressing intent.

Erasure, traced through an actual compile

Here is the input:

import type { Logger } from "./logger";
import { format } from "./format";

interface User { id: string; name: string }
type Status = "active" | "banned";

function describe<T extends User>(user: T, status: Status, log: Logger): string {
  const label = user.name as string;
  return format(label + "!" + status);
}

And here is the entire output:

import { format } from "./format";

function describe(user, status, log) {
  const label = user.name;
  return format(label + "!" + status);
}

Walk through what vanished. The interface — gone, no trace; interfaces never produce anything. The type alias — gone. The generic parameter <T extends User> and its constraint — gone, so at runtime there is exactly one describe function and nothing knows what T was. The parameter annotations and the return annotation — gone. The as string assertion — gone, and note carefully that it did not become a conversion; an assertion emits nothing, it was only ever a message to the compiler. The import type line — gone entirely, which is precisely why that syntax exists (Node 12): it lets you import something that only exists at compile time without leaving a runtime import for a module that may have no runtime content at all.

What remains is JavaScript you might have written by hand. There is no registry of types, no shape descriptor, no check inserted anywhere.

The consequences, stated plainly

You cannot ask what type a value is. There is no if (x is User). The only runtime tools are the JavaScript ones: typeof, which distinguishes eight coarse categories and cannot tell a User from a Product because both answer "object"; and instanceof, which walks the prototype chain and therefore only works for values built by a class or constructor — never for a plain object, and never for one that arrived as JSON. This gap is the entire reason Node 15 exists, and the entire reason Zod exists.

Types cannot change behaviour. Two calls to a generic function with different type arguments run identical code. Nothing is specialised, nothing is generated per type. You cannot write new T(), because T isn't there; if you need construction, you pass a constructor as a value.

instanceof dies at boundaries. Serialise an object to JSON and parse it back, and the prototype is gone — so a custom NotFoundError thrown in a worker, sent through a queue, or returned across HTTP arrives as a plain object with the right properties and the wrong identity. Every instanceof check on it now fails. The fix is a data-based discriminant (Node 4): a literal kind property that survives serialisation because it's just a string. This is one of the most practically useful consequences of erasure and it's worth remembering as a design rule rather than a piece of trivia.

JSON.parse returns any. Which means an annotation on it is accepted without any check whatsoever — the thing Node 15 will call a lie.

Soundness, and why the holes are deliberate

Because assignability is structural and because escape hatches exist, TypeScript accepts programs that will fail at runtime. The published design goals say so outright. The reason is always the same shape of argument: the sound alternative would reject a large amount of JavaScript that works fine in practice, and a checker that cries wolf gets turned off. Every hole you'll meet — bivariant method parameters at Node 6, array covariance at Node 7, assertions and any at Node 9 — is that trade being made again in a different place. Being able to name three of them, and say why each was accepted, is one of the sharpest things you can do in a senior interview, because it demonstrates you understand the tool's purpose rather than just its syntax.

In your project

Stage 2 of recast is this node, made physical, and it's the reason I argued for this project over the others.

A file arrives named invoice.pdf. That name is metadata — a claim, written by whoever last saved the file, checked by nothing. It is exactly a type annotation on external data, and by erasure there is no mechanism anywhere in your program that will verify it. The spec has you demonstrate this in ten seconds by renaming a JPEG to .pdf and watching a converter fail incomprehensibly deep inside a library.

The response is to read the bytes: %PDF at offset zero, \xFF\xD8\xFF for JPEG, the eight-byte PNG signature, ftypheic at offset four. And notice what that is, structurally — it's a runtime check that establishes what you're holding, producing a narrowed type the compiler can then rely on. It's a type predicate (Node 9) over a discriminated union (Node 4), sitting at a boundary (Node 15), and it exists because of erasure. Four nodes converging on the first real feature you build.

Stage 3's converter registry then leans on structural typing in the ordinary way: converters from different libraries with different internal shapes all satisfy one Converter interface without any of them declaring so, which is what makes a registry of heterogeneous implementations possible at all.

And Stage 10 plants the erasure lesson with teeth: transferring an ArrayBuffer to a Web Worker moves ownership, so the sender is left holding a buffer of length zero — while the type still cheerfully says it holds the full thing. The type layer isn't wrong exactly; it simply doesn't exist at the moment ownership moves, and there is no annotation that could have expressed it. That's the most honest single demonstration of erasure you will personally own, which is why the spec makes it an interview line.

In qbank

Two things in qbank are worth re-reading with this node in hand.

Every Drizzle row type is structural. typeof applications.$inferSelect produces an object type, and anything with matching members satisfies it — there is no runtime class, no identity, nothing that marks a value as "a row from this table." That's fine, and it's also why passing a row-shaped object built by hand into a function expecting a row is accepted without comment.

More importantly: every place qbank calls the Anthropic API with forced tool use and reads the returned arguments, erasure is the reason the type you wrote there guarantees nothing. The model returns JSON text; JSON.parse produces any; the annotation is accepted; no check occurs. If the schema and the handler drift, or the model returns a plausible-but-wrong shape, nothing in the type system will notice — and that code currently looks safe. That's the gap this node names and Node 15 closes.

What an interviewer does with this

"What's the difference between structural and nominal typing, and which does TypeScript use?" — extremely common, and the weak answer stops at the definition. Strong: "Structural — compatibility is by shape, not by declared name, so a class instance or an object literal satisfies an interface without declaring anything. It was chosen because TypeScript had to describe JavaScript written before it existed, and a nominal system would have rejected nearly all of it. The cost is that two types with the same shape are interchangeable, so if I need UserId and PostId to be distinct I brand them."

"Do types exist at runtime? How would you check a value's type at runtime?" — this is the screening question for whether someone understands the language or has only used it. No, everything is erased; the only runtime tools are typeof for primitives and instanceof for class instances, neither of which can verify an interface. For real data you validate with a schema and derive the type from it. Someone who answers "I'd use typeof" for an object shape has revealed the boundary of their understanding.

"Why does TypeScript complain about an extra property in an object literal if extra properties are structurally fine?" — excess property checking on fresh literals, added because a fresh literal with an unknown property is almost always a typo. Mentioning that assigning to a variable first bypasses it shows you know it's a freshness heuristic rather than a rule of the type system.

"Is TypeScript's type system sound?" — no, deliberately, and the published design goals list soundness as a non-goal. Name concrete holes — method parameter bivariance, array covariance, assertions, any — and the reason: the sound version would reject too much working JavaScript, and a type checker people disable is worth nothing.

"Your custom error's instanceof check works locally and fails in production. Why?" — a good scenario question. Because the error crossed a serialisation boundary — a queue, a worker, an HTTP response — and the prototype didn't survive. Use a literal discriminant property instead, which is data and therefore survives anything.

sections.title: Node 3 — Object types
sections.content:
Where this sits

Node 1 established that a value's type is a claim the compiler checks. Node 2 established that compatibility is decided by shape and that the whole layer disappears at compile time. This node is where those two facts become a practical tool: naming a shape once and reusing it everywhere, instead of writing { name: string; email: string } at every function signature in your codebase.

Every term, from absolute zero

Object type — a type describing an object's members: their names and their types. { name: string; email: string } is one, written inline — an object type literal.

interface — a keyword that gives an object type a name: interface User { name: string; email: string }. Declares a shape and nothing else; there is no implementation, no value, just a description.

type alias — a keyword that gives any type a name, not only object shapes: type User = { name: string }, but equally type Id = string or type Status = "on" | "off".

Declaration merging — when two declarations with the same name combine into one rather than conflicting. Interfaces do this; type aliases do not.

Optional property — a member that may be absent, marked with ?: email?: string. Its type becomes string | undefined wherever you read it.

readonly modifier — on a property, blocks reassignment as far as the compiler is concerned. Enforced only at compile time.

Index signature — a member describing a whole category of keys at once rather than one named key: { [key: string]: number } means "any string key maps to a number." Used for dictionary-shaped objects where the key set isn't known in advance.

Intersection type — A & B, written with the ampersand, means a value has all the members of both A and B combined.

extends (on an interface) — interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[] } — copies User's members into Admin and adds more. This is the one place extends means something closer to inheritance rather than "is assignable to" (contrast with Node 8's generic constraints, where extends means assignability).

Structural asymmetry — the same real-world entity needing different type shapes depending on which direction it's moving across a boundary. A row you read from a database has an id; a row you're about to insert doesn't yet. You'll meet this precisely at Node 16.

The mechanism, traced

Interface vs type alias: what actually differs

For describing a plain object shape, these two are checked identically by the compiler — same assignability rules, same erasure, no runtime or performance difference at ordinary scale:

interface UserA { name: string; email: string }
type UserB = { name: string; email: string };

A function expecting UserA will happily accept a value typed as UserB and vice versa, because both reduce to the same structural shape (Node 2). The difference is not in what they check — it's in what else they can do.

Interfaces merge. Declare the same interface name twice in one scope and TypeScript combines the members:

interface Config { port: number }
interface Config { host: string }
// Config is now { port: number; host: string }

Type aliases reject this outright — a second type Config = ... in the same scope is a compile error, "duplicate identifier." Merging looks like a curiosity in isolation and turns out to be the entire mechanism behind extending a library's types from your own code, which is Node 17's subject in full.

Type aliases can express things interfaces cannot. An interface can only ever describe an object-like shape (or a function/constructor signature, which is object-like enough). A type alias can name a union (type Status = "pending" | "done"), a tuple, a primitive, or a computed type built from keyof, mapped types, or conditional types — none of which have any "extends" story or make sense as an interface at all.

The working rule, and it's a convention rather than a technical requirement: interfaces for object shapes other code might need to extend, type aliases for everything else. Consistency inside one codebase matters more than which rule you pick.

The three modifiers that carry weight

Optional (?). interface Options { timeout?: number } means a caller may omit timeout. Inside the function, options.timeout has type number | undefined — not number — so using it without a check is an error under strictNullChecks (Node 5). This is the connecting thread to Node 4: an optional property is a two-member union in disguise, and you narrow it exactly the way you'd narrow any union.

readonly. interface Point { readonly x: number } — the compiler rejects p.x = 5 wherever p is typed as Point. It does nothing at runtime: Object.freeze(p) is the actual runtime lock, and the two are unrelated mechanisms that happen to sound similar. A readonly property can still be reassigned through a differently-typed reference to the same object, which is worth knowing so you don't treat it as a security boundary.

Index signatures. interface Scores { [player: string]: number } describes a dictionary: any string key, always a number value. The cost is real — TypeScript now has no idea which keys actually exist, so every read is technically number even for a key you never set (this is exactly what noUncheckedIndexedAccess, from Node 5, exists to make honest by widening reads to number | undefined). Mixing named properties with an index signature requires every named property's type to be compatible with the index signature's value type, or the compiler rejects the combination.

Composition: extends vs intersection

interface User { name: string; email: string }
interface Admin extends User { permissions: string[] }

type UserT = { name: string; email: string };
type AdminT = UserT & { permissions: string[] };

Both give you an object with all three members. The visible difference shows up when something conflicts:

interface A { value: string }
interface B { value: number }
interface C extends A, B { }
// error: interface 'C' cannot simultaneously extend types 'A' and 'B'.
// Named property 'value' types 'string' and 'number' are not identical.

interface extends catches the conflict immediately, at the declaration.

type AT = { value: string };
type BT = { value: number };
type CT = AT & BT;
// CT.value has type: never

The intersection alias doesn't error at the declaration — it just quietly computes value: never, because a value satisfying both string and number simultaneously is impossible, and never is exactly "the type with no values" (fully defined at Node 9). The error only appears later, wherever you actually try to use CT, and by then the message points at a call site far from the real cause. Knowing this in advance is what turns a baffling error into an "oh, right, that's the intersection thing" moment.

The asymmetry that recurs for the rest of the topic

One entity, several shapes, depending on direction:

interface UserRow {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  email: string;
  createdAt: Date;
}

interface NewUser {
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

UserRow is what you get back from a query — it has an id and a timestamp the database generated. NewUser is what you send to create one — no id yet, no timestamp yet, because those don't exist until the database assigns them. They're related (NewUser is a subset of UserRow's writable fields), but they are not the same type, and treating them as if they were is a real source of bugs: code that reads .id off a value that hasn't been inserted yet, or code that requires an id when constructing a new one.

This is worth internalising as a general shape rather than a one-off: an update payload is usually all fields optional (Partial<NewUser>, Node 10); a public API response often hides fields the database holds (an internal passwordHash column has no business in UserRow as returned to a client). You'll meet this exact asymmetry again at Node 16 with Drizzle's $inferSelect versus $inferInsert, which is the same idea with the derivation done for you instead of by hand.

In your project

Stage 2 of recast is where object types first matter for real: a DetectedFile needs one shape per detected kind (a PDF has a page count once opened, a HEIC doesn't), which is the first real argument for a discriminated union of object types rather than one flat interface with everything optional — you'll formalise the "why" at Node 4, but the object-type vocabulary is built here.

Stage 3's converter registry entries are also object types with real structural weight: each entry's options shape differs by conversion (JPEG takes a quality number, PDF split takes a page range), and Stage 5's contract package is the create/read/response asymmetry from this node, applied for real — a job-creation payload, a stored job row, and an API response about that job are three related but distinct object types, exactly like NewUser and UserRow above.

What an interviewer does with this

"Interface or type — what's the actual difference?" — near-universal, and the weak answer stops at "they're basically the same." Strong: "For object shapes, functionally interchangeable — same structural checking, same erasure. The differences that matter are that interfaces merge, which is what lets you extend a library's types from your own code, and type aliases can express unions and computed types that interfaces can't. I use interfaces for shapes I expect to be extended, type aliases for everything else."

"Why did my intersection type produce never instead of an error?" — a real debugging question. Because conflicting members in an intersection resolve to never at the point of conflict rather than failing at the declaration, so the visible error shows up later, at a use site, and can look unrelated to its actual cause.

"How would you model a user you're about to create versus a user you've already fetched?" — checking whether the candidate has actually hit this in practice. A good answer names the asymmetry directly: the created-user type lacks generated fields like an id and timestamps, and treating the two as one shape is how bugs get in where code assumes an id exists before the database has assigned one.
